enrichment.short_title: Frankice v Customs: permission to appeal on gaming machine duty unless order
key_facts: Customs raised about £455,000 in gaming machine licence duty assessments on Frankice (GG) Ltd, which appealed to the VAT and Duties Tribunal.

An unless order required Customs to serve a statement of case by 14 March 2003; a Tribunal letter of 18 March stated the appeal stood allowed, but Customs later proved a fax sent on 13 March and the appeal was restored.
Tribunal member Wallace found on the balance of probabilities that the statement of case was served in time, though list-of-documents compliance was unsatisfactory.
Frankice sought an extension of time to appeal to the High Court some 14 weeks late; Lindsay J refused, and Laws LJ had adjourned the permission application to a two-judge court.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Adjourned application to the Court of Appeal for permission to appeal Lindsay J's refusal to extend time to appeal a VAT and Duties Tribunal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; no real prospect of success on perversity, list-of-documents or irrevocable allowing arguments, and inadequate explanation for gross delay.
enrichment.ratio: Where extension of time is refused for inadequate reasons, an appellate court asks only whether the judge arguably erred in exercising discretion; perversity requires showing no reasonable tribunal could have reached the finding, and a Tribunal administrative letter based on mistaken facts is not an irrevocable decision allowing an appeal.
legal_issues: Whether Wallace's finding that Customs faxed the statement of case on 13 March was perverse
Whether compliance failed because no adequate list of documents was served
Whether the 18 March 2003 letter irrevocably allowed the appeal
Whether Lindsay J erred in refusing an extension of time for lodging the appeal
linked_authorities: Sayers v Clarke Walker [2002] 1 WLR 3095
Ladd v Marshall [1954] 1 WLR 1489

notes: Landmark Hoffmann judgment on MNOPF participating employer liability; comprehensive scheme analysis and clear answers.

enrichment.short_title: MNOPF Trustees v Everard: who is a participating employer for deficiency
key_facts: The Merchant Navy Officers Pension Fund faced a £194m past-service deficiency in its Post-1978 Section as at March 2003.
On 8 June 2000 the trustee amended the rules to widen 'Participating Employers' and inserted Rule 5.2A imposing additional lump-sum or ongoing contributions to cure deficiencies.

Former employers with no active members argued they had ceased participating before the amendment and were not bound, distinguishing employers who still employed merchant navy officers eligible under clause 6.1.
The trustee contended all employers who had ever joined under accession agreements remained liable to future rule variations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim for declarations on construction of the trust deed and rules as to which employers fall within 'Participating Employers' for Rule 5.2A liability.
enrichment.outcome: Declarations that former participating employers without active members remained Participating Employers bound by the 2000 deed, and that Pre-1978 employers were not excluded from Post-1978 deficiency contributions.
enrichment.ratio: Accession agreements bind employers to obligations undertaken by Participating Employers under the trust deed and any subsequent variation; the wide Rule 3 definition applies in the agreements unless context requires otherwise, and sectionalisation of the scheme does not prevent scheme-wide exercise of the trustee's deficiency-remedy powers.
legal_issues: Whether employers who ceased to employ active members before 8 June 2000 remained Participating Employers
Whether accession agreements limited liability to Rule 5.2 contributions for current employers only
Whether Pre-1978 employers could be required to fund Post-1978 Section deficiencies
Construction of clause 30 amendment powers and Rule 29.2 deficiency machinery
linked_authorities: British Airways Pension Trustees Ltd v British Airways Plc [2002] EWCA Civ 672
Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896

notes: GMC fitness-to-practise appeal; suspension decision and insight analysis are fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Mohit v GMC: challenge to 12-month suspension after failed conditional registration
key_facts: Dr Mohit, a Sheffield GP, faced GMC findings of serious professional performance deficiencies across communication, record-keeping, teamwork and related areas, though clinical skills were acceptable.

After suspension the Fitness to Practise Committee in June 2004 imposed six months' conditional registration to allow hospital SHO/locum work under educational supervision instead of general practice.
He failed to obtain an approved hospital post within six months and undertook limited CPD, continuing to dispute many of the original deficiencies.
A December 2004 committee imposed a further 12-month suspension, finding little prospect of improvement through education and insufficient patient-protection under conditional registration.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal from a GMC Fitness to Practise Committee decision refusing further conditional registration and imposing suspension.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the committee was entitled to find insufficient insight, inadequate remedial steps and no safe basis to extend conditional registration; costs summarily assessed at £2,611.70.
enrichment.ratio: Courts intervene in GMC fitness-to-practise sanctions only where the committee's decision is clearly wrong; attitudinal deficiencies affecting patient and colleague communication can justify suspension even where clinical skills are adequate, and persistent lack of insight undermines conditional registration designed to demonstrate improvement.
legal_issues: Whether the committee erred in refusing extra time to secure supervised hospital employment
Whether attitudinal performance defects posed no danger to the public outside general practice
Whether the appellant's CPD and educational activity addressed identified deficiencies
Standard of appellate review of GMC sanction decisions

enrichment.short_title: Sherrington v Sherrington: validity of solicitor's will leaving estate to widow
key_facts: Richard Sherrington, a successful solicitor and businessman, died leaving an estate including Barex Brokers worth about £6m and a substantial pension fund.
His widow Yvonne propounded a short will leaving everything to her; his three adult children from his first marriage challenged validity.
The will was signed at Sherringtons' office before cleaner Mr Thakkar and Mrs Butt, who gave evidence they did not see the deceased sign or intend to attest.
The trial judge held due execution and knowledge/approval were not proved, so the deceased died intestate; the Court of Appeal regarded intestacy as fairer but upheld the will on law.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by the widow against revocation of probate after a six-day probate trial; cross-appeal on alternative execution ground.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and grant of probate to Yvonne quashed; will validly executed and deceased knew and approved contents; children's cross-appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: The presumption of due execution from a signed will with an attestation clause requires the strongest evidence to rebut; witnesses need not know the document is a will but must attest the signature, and where a capable solicitor had opportunity to read a short will without suspicion of undue influence, knowledge and approval will readily be inferred.
legal_issues: Whether section 9 Wills Act 1837 attestation requirements were satisfied
Whether witnesses intended to attest the testator's signature
Whether the deceased knew and approved will contents excluding his children
Application of Barry v Butlin suspicious circumstances doctrine
linked_authorities: Barry v Butlin (1838) 2 Moo PC 480
Fuller v Strum [2002] 1 WLR 1097
Smith & Smith v Smith (1869) LR 1 P&D 143

enrichment.short_title: Cornwall Crescent v RBKC: validity of landlord's enfranchisement counter-notice price

statutes_considered.title: Leasehold Reform, Housing and Urban Development Act 1993

key_facts: Tenants' nominee served a section 13 initial notice proposing £210 for collective enfranchisement of flats in Kensington.
The Royal Borough admitted the right but counter-proposed £130,000 based on in-house valuer advice; the valuer later accepted the figure was not an open-market valuation.
Tenants sought a declaration that the counter-notice was invalid as unrealistically high so they could acquire at £210 under Willingale v Globalgrange default rules.
The county court held Cadogan v Morris realism applied; the Court of Appeal reversed on statutory construction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court declaration that the landlord's section 21 counter-notice was invalid for proposing an unrealistic purchase price.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Cadogan v Morris realism requirement applies to tenants' initial notices but not to landlords' section 21 counter-proposals, which need only specify a counter-proposal for tribunal determination.
enrichment.ratio: Section 25 default consequences justify qualifying tenants' proposed prices under Cadogan v Morris, but a landlord's section 21 counter-proposal has no equivalent default effect and complies with the Act if it states a figure put forward for consideration, however high, leaving price disputes to the leasehold valuation tribunal.
legal_issues: Whether Cadogan v Morris 'realistic price' test applies to a section 21 counter-notice
Whether an objectively excessive but bona fide valuer-backed counter-proposal invalidates the notice
Distinction between section 13 and section 21 legal consequences under Willingale
Relevance of Sun Life Assurance v Thales Tracs to 'proposal' meaning
linked_authorities: Cadogan v Morris [1999] 1 EGLR 59
Willingale v Globalgrange Ltd [2000] 2 EGLR 55
Sun Life Assurance plc v Thales Tracs Ltd [2001] 1 WLR 1562

enrichment.short_title: Wainwright v NWDA: challenge to Kingsway Business Park compulsory purchase
key_facts: The North West Development Agency sought compulsory purchase of land including Dig Gate Barn plots for rerouting footpath 358 after M62 underpass closure for the Kingsway Business Park, Rochdale.
Inspector Linscott upheld Mr Wainwright's objection only to the extent land-take was excessive, recommending modification to a 1.3m path with hedge.
Post-inquiry the Secretary of State invited views on modifying plots 69–71; Wainwright proposed an alternative route rather than commenting on NWDA's reduced land-take.
The Secretary of State confirmed the order with NWDA's modified plots, requiring full title for construction works and hedge required by planning condition.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 23 Acquisition of Land Act 1981 application by a litigant in person challenging confirmation of a compulsory purchase order affecting his property.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no legal or procedural flaw in the decision letter; fresh post-inquiry alternatives could not be reheard; costs summarily assessed at £10,000 (Secretary of State) and £25,000 (NWDA).
enrichment.ratio: A section 23 challenge is not a merits rehearing; objectors must identify legal or procedural error in the confirming decision, and post-inquiry alternative routes or belated freehold-versus-easement arguments raised only after the inquiry cannot vitiate a proportionate CPO decision implementing an inspector's modified recommendation.
legal_issues: Whether a replacement footpath was unnecessary because existing footpaths sufficed
Whether NWDA lacked power under section 20(1) RDA Act and should have used section 20(2) rights only
Lawfulness of rejecting Wainwright's post-inquiry alternative route
Whether full freehold acquisition rather than a licence was necessary for the diverted footpath

enrichment.short_title: Palmac v Park Lane: enforcing adjudicator's interim payment decision

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: Palmac contracted with Park Lane on JCT Design and Build 1998 for airport property works and referred payment application 20 for £748,447.64 to adjudication after no payment or withholding notice.
First adjudication failed for non-service of notice; a second notice was served on 15 December 2004 and Eric Mouzer was re-nominated, deciding £169,912.85 plus VAT was due.
Park Lane resisted enforcement for lack of dispute, invalid appointment timing and natural justice breach over service of application 20 by email.
The adjudicator held application 20 validly served and that agreement by conduct made Nicol Thomas the effective recipient.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court summary judgment application to enforce an adjudicator's decision on interim payment application 20.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment granted; no real prospect of defending enforcement on jurisdiction or natural justice grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Whether an interim application was validly served is a merits question within adjudicator jurisdiction; clause 39A.2.2 does not require RICS nomination only after notice of adjudication is served, and an adjudicator may rely on party submissions on agreement by conduct without breaching natural justice where both parties had opportunity to comment.
legal_issues: Whether a dispute existed where application 20 was emailed to the employer's agent
Whether nomination before service of notice of adjudication invalidated appointment under clause 39A.2.2
Whether the adjudicator breached natural justice by finding service by conduct without prior warning
Application of Thomas-Fredric's principles to summary enforcement

enrichment.short_title: Saghir v Najib: Calderdale postal-vote election petition struck out

statutes_considered.title: European Parliamentary and Local Elections (Pilot) Act 2004

key_facts: Three Conservative candidates petitioned to challenge Labour victories in Calderdale Park Ward at the June 2004 all-postal pilot local election.
They filed version 1 of the petition but served version 2 on respondents; their 30 June letter claimed security paid before it was actually paid on 2 July.
Alleged improprieties included postal vote collection, counting without agents and an unbelievable turnout, but particulars remained vague.
The returning officer and elected councillors applied to strike out for non-compliance with section 136 notice requirements and hopeless particulars.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Strike-out applications against a local election petition after adjournment and appointment of an advocate to the court.
enrichment.outcome: Petition struck out for failure to serve prescribed notice of presentation and security within time under Ahmed v Kennedy; would also have failed for lack of particularity and no prospect of success.
enrichment.ratio: Election petition Rules 1960 and section 136 impose mandatory timeous service of notice of the petition actually presented and of security given; non-compliance is not curable under CPR discretion and nullifies the petition, and vague allegations of postal-vote malpractice without cogent evidence cannot survive strike-out.
legal_issues: Whether version 2 service satisfied notice requirements when only version 1 was presented
Whether pre-payment letter or later 6 July letter constituted notice of security under section 136(3)
Whether CPR 3.10 could cure defective election petition service
Whether petition grounds were sufficiently particularised and had real prospect of success
linked_authorities: Ahmed v Kennedy [2002] EWCA Civ 1793
In re Bristol South East Parliamentary Election [1961] 2 QB 459

enrichment.short_title: Beaulane v Palmer: adverse possession and Human Rights Act reinterpretation
key_facts: Beaulane owned a Green Belt field near Heathrow; Mr Palmer claimed title by 12 years' grazing horses and cattle from October 1986, charging others for livery.
Beaulane disputed sufficient exclusive possession and argued limitation did not run until June 1991 because Palmer concealed his trespass from agents.
If 12 years completed in June 2003, Pye-style acquisition after the Human Rights Act 2000 raised Article 1 Protocol 1 compatibility issues.
Following Pye v Graham, the court considered whether limitation/bar rules expropriated registered owners without compensation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of claim for possession and declaration of title where squatter relied on adverse possession and owner invoked HRA section 3 reinterpretation.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration that Beaulane remains owner; Palmer's adverse possession claim fails after section 3-compatible reading of section 75 Land Registration Act 1925 preventing retrospective expropriation.
enrichment.ratio: Where adverse possession would retrospectively bar a registered owner's title in breach of Article 1 Protocol 1, section 3 HRA may reinterpret section 75 LRA 1925 so limitation bars the remedy for possession during the expired period without transferring title, preserving the owner's registered ownership.
legal_issues: Whether Palmer had factual exclusive possession for the requisite period
Whether deliberate concealment delayed limitation under section 32 Limitation Act 1980
Compatibility of pre-2002 adverse possession law with Article 1 Protocol 1
Whether section 3 reinterpretation of section 75 LRA 1925 avoids incompatibility

R v A (No 2) [2001] UKHL 25

enrichment.short_title: Whitbread v HMRC: VAT on cold airport sandwiches in departure lounges
key_facts: Costa Ltd, a Whitbread subsidiary, sold cold pre-packaged sandwiches and similar items from airport departure-lounge concessions.
HMRC treated all airside cold food as standard-rated catering supplied for consumption on the premises, rejecting a £235,310.69 repayment claim.
The VAT Tribunal found dedicated seating at some outlets made the service ordinary catering; alternatively the whole departure area was premises under Note (3).
Whitbread argued the concession area alone was premises and that sales to airline staff and passengers buying for in-flight consumption should be zero-rated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal on a point of law from a VAT Tribunal decision refusing repayment of overpaid VAT on cold food sales at UK airports.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on the evidence before the tribunal; departure lounge may constitute premises for Note (3), but zero-rating may apply to staff-discount and buy-for-aircraft sales if evidenced.
enrichment.ratio: Whether airport cold-food sales are catering is largely a question of fact; where outlets provide dedicated seating for a closed group of air travellers the supply is catering, and the entire airside departure area may be 'premises' for extended Note (3) catering even for take-away sales, though supplies clearly not for on-premises consumption (e.g. airline staff or food bought solely to eat on the aircraft) are not catering if proved.
legal_issues: Whether Costa's airside sales were catering in the ordinary sense
Whether the whole departure lounge is premises under Schedule 8 Group 1 Note (3)
Zero-rating of cold food sold to airline employees with discount cards
Zero-rating of food purchased by passengers for consumption on low-cost flights
linked_authorities: Customs and Excise Commissioners v Cope [1981] STC 532
Re Travellers Fare Ltd v CEC (VAT Tribunal)
Armstrong v CEC (VAT Tribunal)
